opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think one of the things we were really deliberate about was keeping the tools as simple and general as possible. For SWE-bench, the agent basically has two tools: a bash tool and a file editing tool. And that's it. We didn't build some elaborate scaffold with specialized tools for searching the repo, or running tests, or navigating the codebase. The philosophy was really: give the model the same kinds of primitives a human engineer would have, and then let the model figure out how to use them.

And I think that's actually a big part of why it generalizes. If you over-engineer the scaffold for one benchmark, you end up encoding a lot of your own assumptions about how the task should be solved, and that tends to break as soon as you go to a slightly different problem. Whereas bash is incredibly general. You can grep, you can run the tests, you can write a little script to reproduce the bug. The model gets to choose.

The edit tool is where we actually spent a lot of time, though. It's a string-replace style tool, where the model specifies the exact text to replace and what to replace it with. We tried a bunch of variants, like line-number-based edits or diffs, and the models just made more mistakes with those. Something I'd emphasize to anyone building agents is to spend as much time on the tool interface as you would on a prompt. Write the tool descriptions like you're writing docs for a junior engineer, think about the error messages, make it hard for the model to shoot itself in the foot. Like, we required absolute file paths because relative paths caused confusion once the agent had cd'ed somewhere.

And computer use is kind of the same idea taken further. Instead of building integrations for every app, you give the model a screen, a mouse, and a keyboard, the most general interface there is, since every piece of software already has to work for humans through it. It's less efficient than an API when one exists, for sure, but the generality is the point. The more the model improves, the more these simple, general tools pay off, versus brittle hand-built pipelines that you'd have to keep rewriting.

r001.rationale: It describes bash and file editing as simple, general-purpose primitives, and gives examples of bash handling repository search, tests, and bug reproduction.

r002.rationale: It explicitly favors bash and file editing over specialized scaffold tools, including a dedicated tool for running tests.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that's interesting about both of those is that we tried really hard to keep the tools as simple and general as possible, and a lot of the work was actually on the model side rather than the tool side.

For the SWE-bench setup, the whole thing is essentially a bash tool and a file editing tool. That's it. There's no fancy repo mapping, no special retrieval system, no planning scaffold. The agent gets a terminal and the ability to view and edit files, and the rest is the model deciding what to do. And we found that the more structure we tried to bake into the scaffold, the more we were actually constraining the model in ways that hurt it. The model is already pretty good at figuring out "I should grep for this function, then look at the tests, then run them." If you try to hard-code that workflow, you end up with something that works great on the cases you anticipated and falls over on the ones you didn't.

Computer use is kind of the extreme version of that philosophy. The tools there are literally screenshot, move the mouse, click, type. It's the lowest common denominator interface that a human uses. And the reason we went that direction instead of building a bunch of app-specific integrations is that generality is the whole point. There are a huge number of pieces of software out there with no API, and if you can operate the GUI, you can in principle use any of them. You're not waiting on someone to build an integration.

The tradeoff, of course, is that it's slower and more error-prone than a purpose-built tool. If you have a clean API for something, you should absolutely use it. I think the way to think about it is that computer use is a fallback that covers the long tail, and specific tools are what you reach for when they exist. And the nice thing is those compose. You can give the model a bash tool, a file editor, and a screen, and it will pick the right one for the job.

The other thing I'd say is that a lot of the "generality" really lives in the model. We trained on these simple primitives because we want the model to be good at working through problems with whatever it has available, rather than being dependent on a particular harness. So when someone takes our SWE-bench scaffold and swaps in their own tools, it mostly just works, because the model has learned the general skill of being an agent rather than a specific choreography.

r001.rationale: It describes the SWE-bench tools as a bash tool plus file editing, giving the model a terminal and the ability to view and edit files, and characterizes this setup as simple and general.

r002.rationale: It favors simple bash and file-editing tools over baked-in scaffolding, and says the model can use the terminal to find code, inspect tests, and run them.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting thing is how much you can do with a relatively small set of general tools. For SWE-bench, you can give the model a way to run commands, read files, and edit code. Those aren’t tools that encode how to fix a particular bug; they give the model access to the environment, and it has to figure out the solution.

Computer use takes that idea a step further. If the model can look at a screenshot and use a mouse and keyboard, it can potentially interact with a lot of different software without us building a custom integration for each application. That’s a very general interface.

Of course, having access to the interface doesn’t mean it can reliably do every task. There’s still a big gap between being able to click and type and being able to carry out a long workflow correctly. But the direction is to put more of the intelligence in the model, so the tools can stay relatively simple.

r001.rationale: It describes command execution and file reading/editing as a small set of general tools that give the model access to the environment and can be used without encoding a particular fix.

r002.rationale: It favors simple, general-purpose tools that leave the model to figure out the solution, rather than tools that encode a specific SWE-bench action or fix.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting thing is how little of the tooling needs to be specific to the task. For SWE-bench, you can give the model a terminal and a way to read and edit files, and then it has to figure out how to explore the repository, reproduce the issue, make a change, and test it. You’re not building a separate tool for every kind of bug.

Computer use takes that a step further. The interface is screenshots, mouse clicks, and keyboard input—the same interface a person uses. That potentially lets the model work with a lot of existing software without someone having to build an API integration for each application.

Of course, having a general interface doesn’t mean you’re reliable at every task. But it changes where the engineering goes: you can improve the model’s ability to reason and recover from mistakes, and those improvements can help across many different workflows.

r001.rationale: The response describes terminal and file reading/editing tools as sufficient for repository exploration, reproducing issues, making changes, and testing, and says little tooling needs to be task-specific. This conveys their broad generality.

r002.rationale: The response favors using a terminal and file tools to handle the work instead of building a separate tool for each kind of bug, communicating a preference for general-purpose tools over task-specific ones.
